title: Isomorphic strings
label: idb-list
statement: Two strings are **isomorphic** if you can rename the characters of the first, consistently and one-for-one, to get the second. Every occurrence of a character must become the same character, and two different characters may not become the same one.
provenance: **InterviewDB-listed.** LeetCode 205 is on the LinkedIn list you supplied from InterviewDB. No candidate report of this exact question was found in the research passes — the evidence is that the list names it. On that list it uses the same pattern as InterviewDB Q11. A stronger link than it looks. Q11’s keypad signature is a character → class mapping used to build a canonical key; isomorphism checks whether such a mapping exists. Both are the "reduce to a canonical form, then compare in O(1)" move.

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md: Two strings are **isomorphic** if you can rename the characters of the first, consistently and one-for-one, to get the second. Every occurrence of a character must become the same character, and two different characters may not become the same one.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
- Same length required? (Yes.)
- Can a character map to itself? (Yes.)
- Character set? (Any char.)

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md: One map is not enough: "badc" → "baba" passes a forward check (b→b, a→a, d→b, c→a) but d and b both become b. Keep a map in each direction, or compare "first index where each character appears".

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md: I would say, before coding: "T."wo maps, s→t and t→s, checked and filled in one pass; any conflict in either direction is a no — O(n)."

learn.title: 11 · AI usage strategy
learn.md:
- Make the design decision yourself, then ask the assistant to attack it.
- Delegate the mechanical parts only after the structure is fixed.

**Prompts for this question:**

- *Check my design — no code* — "I believe two maps, s→t and t→s, checked and filled in one pass; any conflict in either direction is a no — O(n). Review my reasoning without giving me the implementation. What would break it?"
- *Review, do not rewrite* — "Review my implementation for correctness and edge cases. Do not rewrite the code. List problems most severe first, each with the input that triggers it."
- *Race conditions* — "Now review this implementation for race conditions if multiple threads call Check concurrently. For each race, give the interleaving that breaks it. Then name the smallest synchronization boundary that preserves correctness. Do not write code yet."
- *Tests that expose bugs* — "Suggest tests that could expose bugs in my implementation: boundaries, duplicates, empty and invalid input, and concurrency where it applies. For each, say why the expected value is correct."
- *Complexity check* — "What is the time and space complexity of each public method as written? Do not claim a bound unless every step achieves it."

learn.title: 12 · Common AI mistakes
learn.md:
- Only checking s → t, missing two letters mapping to one.
- Fixed 26-letter arrays when the input can contain any character.
- Forgetting the length check.
